newsitem.title: USA: G24 supports special SDR issue, IMF gold sales.
newsitem.headline: G24 supports special SDR issue, IMF gold sales.

text.p: The G24 group of developing countries Saturday said it supported a proposal for a special issue of SDRs, the International Monetary Fund's artificial currency, totalling about $38 billion.

Finance ministers, central bank governors and economic officials of the G24, which mostly groups countries from Africa, Asia and Latin America, met here during the annual meeting of the IMF and the World Bank.
"In the spirit of solidarity, ministers were prepared to support a one-time move to equalize the ratio of cumulative SDR allocation to present quotas," a G24 communique said.
Their support would break a two-year-long deadlock over the issuance of Special Drawing Rights (SDRs) for the IMF's newest members, the so-called "transition" countries such as Russia.
SDRs allow member countries to beef up their currency reserves and effectively boost their borrowing power.
Industrialized countries had proposed in 1994 to issue 16 billion SDRs, equivalent to about $23 billion, and allot them solely to transition countries.
The G24, however, effectively blocked that plan, arguing that the IMF's charter only allowed for general allocations.
The IMF's staff recently came up with a compromise solution, proposing a special issue to bring all member countries to the same ratio of SDRs to their membership quotas.

Although that ratio has not yet been set, G24 chairman Qazi Alimullah of Pakistan told a news conference the developing countries backed IMF Managing Director Michel Camdessus' suggested benchmark ratio of 33 percent of quotas.
Alimullah, who is deputy chairman of the Pakistani Planning Commission, said that such a solution would entail an issue of around 26.6 billion SDRs, worth about $38 billion.

The G24 also said it supported the sale of IMF gold reserves to prop up the Fund's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility (ESAF), an IMF loan program earmarked for both transition and highly indebted poor countries.
